title: Path Sum: given a tree and a target, determine if any root-to-leaf path sums to the target. Path Sum III: count the number of downward paths (not necessarily starting at the root or ending at a leaf) whose values sum to the target.
shortTitle: Path Sum / Path Sum III: root-to-leaf path / all downward paths summing to target
keyPoints: Path Sum subtracts each node's value from the target and checks for zero at a leaf
Path Sum III uses a prefix-sum HashMap to count all downward paths summing to the target in O(n)
The naive Path Sum III approach explores all paths from every node in O(n * h) time
The prefix-sum map must be decremented on backtrack so counts do not leak across sibling branches
Seeding the map with prefix sum 0 having count 1 handles paths starting from the root
Use long for the running sum to avoid integer overflow with large node values

s1_definition.oneliner: Path Sum subtracts toward a leaf; Path Sum III uses a running prefix sum and a HashMap so each node counts matching downward paths in constant time.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Path Sum** checks if any root-to-leaf path sums to a target by subtracting each node's value and testing zero at a leaf.
- **Path Sum III** counts all downward paths (any start, any end) summing to the target.
- **Prefix-sum HashMap** maps running sums to their frequency on the current root-to-node path.
- **Key insight** is that a path from ancestor A to current node C sums to target when `prefixSum(C) - prefixSum(A) == target`.
- **Backtracking** decrements the map on return to prevent counts from leaking across branches.
- **Time** is O(n) with the map; **space** is O(h) for the map entries and call stack.
s1_definition.analogy: Path Sum is like asking whether any single chain of command from the branch manager down to a frontline employee at the National Bank of India has salaries adding up to a budget figure. Path Sum III is harder: it counts every downward stretch of the chain, not just full top-to-bottom ones, whose salaries hit the figure. To count those efficiently, as you walk down a chain you remember every running total you have seen, so when the current total overshoots the target by an amount you have seen before, you know a matching stretch ends right here.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Path Sum III: prefix-sum technique
  ====================================

  Tree:        10          Target = 8
              / \
             5   -3
            / \    \
           3   2    11

  Walk from root to node 3 (left-left):
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  At 10: runSum=10, map={0:1, 10:1}      │
  │    At 5: runSum=15, map={0:1, 10:1, 15:1}│
  │      At 3: runSum=18                     │
  │        lookup 18-8=10 → count=1 (found!) │
  │        The path [5,3] sums to 8          │
  │      Backtrack: remove 18 from map       │
  │    Backtrack: remove 15 from map         │
  │  ...continues to right subtree...        │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────┘

  Key formula:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  count += map.get(runningSum - target)   │
  │  If runSum - target exists in map,       │
  │  a matching downward path ends here.     │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Path Sum and Path Sum III are a pair that shows how a small change in the question demands a very different technique. Path Sum asks only whether a full root-to-leaf chain adds up to a target, solved by subtracting each node's value from the remaining target and checking for zero at a leaf. It is O(n) and short-circuits on the first match.

Path Sum III counts every downward path that sums to the target, not just full root-to-leaf ones. The efficient solution uses prefix sums: as you walk the current root-to-node path you keep a running sum, and a downward path ending at the current node hits the target when some ancestor had a prefix sum equal to `runningSum - target`. A HashMap tracks the frequency of each prefix sum on the current path.

The step that separates correct implementations from buggy ones is the backtracking: when you return from a node, you decrement its running sum from the map so the prefix sums of an abandoned branch never leak into a sibling branch. Seeding the map with zero counted once handles root-starting paths, and using `long` for the running sum prevents overflow.

At the National Bank of India, Rajesh modeled linked transactions as a tree and used Path Sum III to count every downward sub-chain summing to a suspicious amount, catching structured laundering that hides the target inside a longer chain.

Remember one sentence: Path Sum subtracts toward a leaf, Path Sum III uses a prefix-sum HashMap with backtracking, and the backtrack step is what makes the count correct.
